Kratom Legality by State

Banned in 11 states · regulated in 21 · legal in the other 18 and D.C. — every state on one clickable map, with the laws and the receipts. Updated November 21, 2026.

⚖️ The Short Answer

Kratom is legal in most of the United States — but the map is splitting three ways. 11 states ban it outright, 21 states regulate it under Kratom Consumer Protection Acts and similar laws (age limits, labeling, testing, seller registration), and it is legal with no state framework in 18 states and D.C. The fastest-moving fight is not over the leaf at all — it is over 7-OH, the concentrated alkaloid sold in shots, gummies and tablets, which a growing list of states — and now the DEA — treat as a drug of its own. Green diamonds on the map mark the states with a separate 7-OH rule.

🏛️ The Federal Picture
  • Kratom leaf and mitragynine are NOT federally scheduled. The DEA moved to schedule kratom in 2016 and withdrew the proposal after public and congressional pushback.
  • Since August 26, 2026, three lab-made kratom relatives — mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, MGM-15 and MGM-16 — are temporary Schedule I substances (through August 2028).
  • Concentrated 7-OH is next: the DEA's October 14, 2026 notice of intent (91 FR 65370) would place 7-OH above a threshold — more than 1 mg per gram, or a mitragynine-to-7-OH ratio under 100:1 — in Schedule I. The ruling can publish any day on or after November 13, 2026 and takes effect the day it appears. As of November 21, 2026 it had not yet appeared. Natural leaf below the threshold is expressly outside the action.
  • The FDA has never approved kratom for any use, treats it as an unlawful dietary ingredient and unsafe food additive, and detains imports under Import Alert 54-15 (last revised August 17, 2026). FDA and HHS formally recommended scheduling concentrated 7-OH on July 29, 2025.

📖 How to Read the Map
  • Banned — kratom or its alkaloids are scheduled / prohibited statewide.
  • Regulated — legal to sell under a consumer-protection law: age floor, labeling, testing and/or registration.
  • Legal — no statewide ban and no consumer-protection framework.
  • 7-OH rule — a separate law targets concentrated / synthetic 7-OH even where leaf is legal.

Tap or click any state — on the map, in the banned list, or in the A–Z buttons — for its detail, citation and sources. The small Northeast states sit in the callout column at the right of the map.

⚠️ Local Bans & Traps
  • Denver, Colorado bans kratom sales citywide even though Colorado regulates it statewide.
  • Sarasota County, Florida bans it inside an otherwise regulated state; San Diego, Oceanside and Newport Beach, California ban it locally too.
  • California trap: no state statute — but the state health department treats kratom sold for human consumption as unlawful, so most retailers will not ship there.
  • Spokane, Washington banned sales in March 2026; some Mississippi counties and New York counties (Rensselaer, Oneida) have local bans as well.
  • Travel rule: possession laws follow the state you are standing in — a legal-state purchase is still contraband across a banned-state line.
👀 Watch List — What Changes Next
  • Kentucky — July 1, 2027: a 2026 law (HB 757) ends all kratom sales statewide on that date; possession is not criminalized. Kentucky is regulated until then.
  • Federal 7-OH ruling — any day: the DEA temporary scheduling ruling for high-potency 7-OH and MP could publish any weekday on or after November 13, 2026. Natural leaf below the thresholds is expressly excluded.
  • North Dakota — 2027: licensed 21+ sales of natural kratom begin once the Attorney General’s licensing rules are finished (expected around March 2027); sales stay prohibited until then.
  • Massachusetts — August 2027: the emergency ban expires unless lawmakers replace it; it is already being challenged in court.
  • Pending ban bills: Michigan (passed the House), Hawaii and Iowa have live ban proposals — all three states are legal today.

◆ Why 7-OH Is Treated Differently

An extract and a 7-OH product are not the same kind of thing. The difference is which alkaloids get concentrated — and the law keys on exactly that.

🌿 Full-Spectrum Extract

Concentrated leaf — the whole spectrum, together

Mitragynine — dominant

Schematic: in leaf — and in anything honestly extracted from it — 7-OH is a trace sliver of the alkaloid profile.

  • Made by extracting leaf, so every alkaloid concentrates together, in roughly the proportions the leaf grew with.
  • Mitragynine stays dominant and 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) stays a trace — the same balance as the plant itself.
  • Regulators treat a true extract as concentrated leaf, because the ratio is the leaf's own.

◆ Refined 7-OH

One compound, isolated and amplified

7-OH — the main event

Schematic: refined products invert the leaf's ratio — proportions vary by product, the inversion does not.

  • Made by singling out 7-OH — usually by converting mitragynine into it — and pushing it far beyond anything leaf contains.
  • Because 7-OH is a much more potent opioid-receptor agonist than mitragynine, inverting the ratio changes the character of the product, not just its strength.
  • That inversion is what laws target when they regulate 7-OH as a substance of its own.
⚖️ The federal line

The DEA's pending 7-OH action draws the boundary by ratio: more than 1 mg of 7-OH per gram, or a mitragynine-to-7-OH ratio under 100:1, counts as a concentrated product rather than leaf. Natural leaf and true extracts sit far on the other side of that line.

That is why the map carries two kinds of marks: 8 jurisdictions in this guide flag 7-OH separately while leaf stays legal there. The legal split runs along the ratio — not the plant.

🏛️ The Federal Level — Both Parties Have Held the Pen

2016
The DEA under President Obama — Democrat

Federal regulators announced plans to place kratom in Schedule I — then withdrew the plan after pushback from members of Congress in both parties and a flood of public comments.

2025–26
Federal agencies under President Trump — Republican

The FDA and HHS recommended scheduling concentrated 7-OH in July 2025, and temporary scheduling actions followed in 2026. Natural kratom leaf remains unscheduled at the federal level.

🗳️ Two Governors, Two Parties, Same Year

Kim Reynolds — Iowa

Republican governor

At a September 1, 2026 press conference, Gov. Reynolds called for a total kratom ban — in a state where kratom is legal today. A 2027 rematch is expected.

Kathy Hochul — New York

Democratic governor

A bill capping 7-OH in kratom products passed both chambers and was delivered to Gov. Hochul on November 13, 2026. Her signature or veto is the next move.

📊 Lopsided Votes That Tell the Story

Pennsylvania House — HB 2657, a regulation bill (registration, 21+, synthetics banned)202–0

Unanimous in October 2026 — every member of both parties voted yes.

Michigan House — HB 5537, a statewide ban56–48

Passed by eight votes in March 2026 — closely divided, and still awaiting Senate action.

Delaware Senate — HS 1 for HB 332, a consumer-protection law (21+ age floor)19–0

Unanimous in the Senate in July 2026; the Delaware House passed it 39–1, and the governor signed it on September 8, 2026.

Congress shows the same pattern: federal kratom consumer-protection bills have drawn sponsors and co-sponsors from both parties.

Red states and blue states have banned kratom. Red states and blue states have regulated it. Members of both parties have defended the leaf. On this issue the map is not red or blue — it is red, amber and green.

Merrimack, New HampshireMet Thu Nov 19 — outcome awaited

The Town Council’s final reading of Chapter 195, Kratom Prohibition was set for Thursday, November 19 at 7:00 PM — but as of the November 21 morning check, no outcome or minutes from that meeting had been reported. The draft would ban selling, giving or displaying kratom extracts, enhanced products and semi-synthetic derivatives — 7-OH included — while natural, unadulterated leaf and ground leaf stay exempt for buyers 21+. Draft minutes put fines starting at $250 per item. The council tabled the measure on November 5 (6–0, one abstention) after Eric Evans, an attorney for the American Kratom Association, wrote to the town threatening declaratory and injunctive court relief; the town attorney asked for time to review. Nothing is decided — a small town has become a big test case for local bans.

Statuses are stated as of November 21, 2026. Laws in this area are changing monthly — a state marked legal can ban kratom in a single legislative session.
